paras: The attempted lynching of John Brinkley took place in Chicago on the night of September 8, 1903, when a crowd chased, held and whipped Brinkley, a Black watchman, minutes after, according to the Associated Press, he had shot and killed a plasterer, Charles McCarthy. Four policemen fought through a shower of bricks and stones to carry Brinkley to a police station alive, and none of the crowd was arrested. The wire story ran across the country, and the Black weekly Professional World called it the first Chicago case in which police were "hardly able" to save a prisoner from a mob.

Brinkley, described in the dispatches as "a colored watchman," was employed at a tile factory and had quarters of his own. According to the dispatch, the shooting, which took place almost in the presence of McCarthy's wife, grew out of a quarrel in which McCarthy had accused Brinkley of stealing chickens.

A crowd the Associated Press put at 200 men and boys gathered, and Brinkley backed into the doorway of his quarters and held it at bay with his weapon. Patrolman Robert Mooney walked up to him, unarmed according to most versions, and took the weapon away. Mooney then brought Brinkley into the tile factory office to wait for a patrol wagon, but the crowd surged forward with cries of "Lynch him" and "Get a rope."

The policeman tried without success to hold the office door shut, and while he struggled Brinkley fled through a rear door. Headed by Mooney, the crowd streamed down an alley after him and overtook him several blocks away, brushing the policeman aside. While a dozen men and boys held Brinkley, a teamster jumped down from his wagon and lashed him across the face with a whip.

As the crowd tried to drag Brinkley away, three more policemen arrived in a patrol wagon and with Mooney clubbed their way through while bricks and stones fell on them. The four officers dragged Brinkley into the wagon and drove him to the police station, which the Professional World's version identified as the Maxwell street station. There, according to the dispatch, Brinkley fainted from terror and, when revived, begged to be put in a cell where no mob could reach him.

None of the rioters was arrested, and the dispatch closed by noting that McCarthy's family was left destitute by his death. No report of an inquest into McCarthy's death, of a trial of Brinkley, or of any action against members of the crowd appears in the coverage.

The story went out on the Associated Press wire under a Chicago dateline of September 9 and ran that day in the Providence News, the Topeka State Journal and the Evening Star, among other papers. Over the next several days it appeared in the Omaha Daily Bee, the Raleigh News & Observer and the Atlanta Constitution. Two South Carolina weeklies, the Manning Times and the Watchman and Southron of Sumter, printed it on September 16.

Every white version called Brinkley a "negro murderer," though headlines differed in emphasis. Some stressed the rescue, as in the Topeka State Journal's "Saved From Lynchers" and the Watchman and Southron's "A Negro Murderer Rescued," while the Butte Inter Mountain wrote of "Infuriated Citizens" trying to reach "the Slayer and Kill Him." The Minneapolis Journal said the "Negro Murderer Is Almost Torn to Pieces," the Manning Times titled it "The Negro in Chicago," and the Richmond Times Dispatch added "Because Negro Killed White Man," the only statement of McCarthy's race in the coverage.

The Hopkinsville Kentuckian drew a lesson from it in an editorial note on the imprisonment of twelve white participants in a mob at Danville, Illinois. The paper argued that the Chicago rescue, on "the very day" the Danville men went to the penitentiary, showed such prosecutions would not stop mob law, and warned that more such verdicts could bring "a general race war."

In the Black press the episode appears only in the Professional World of September 18, under the headline "Almost Lynch a Negro." Its text followed the wire's wording, including "negro murderer" and a killing "done in cold blood," but bore a Chicago dateline of September 16 and named the Maxwell street station. It added a paragraph, without further comment, noting that Chicago had seen many "inconsequential cases" of threatened lynching, but none in which a crime stirred "such indignation and race hatred" that police could barely save the prisoner.

The versions differ on the date: the September 9 dispatch placed the attack "last night," the Manning Times said "Wednesday night," and the Professional World's version, datelined September 16, also said "last night." Because the story was already in print on September 9, the night of September 8 given by the original dispatch is the best supported date.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of John Brinkley
bases: A crowd crying 'Lynch him' and 'Get a rope' chased, held and whipped Brinkley, a prisoner accused of murder, and tried to drag him away before police rescued him: an attempted lynching (A3, A4, A17).

A crowd of men and boys, a dozen of whom held Brinkley, tried to lynch him in retaliation for the killing of McCarthy, but four policemen took him to the station alive, so no one was killed (A4, A17, A23).
Every report, including the Black-press version, derives from one Associated Press dispatch from Chicago; no independent local or eyewitness account was found (A2, A17, A23).

accounts.label: Associated Press dispatch from Chicago
accounts.gist: Brinkley shot McCarthy, held a crowd of 200 at bay, was disarmed by Mooney, escaped from the factory office as the crowd cried for lynching, and was whipped by the crowd until four policemen fought through bricks and stones to take him to the station; no rioters were arrested.

accounts.label: Professional World version
accounts.gist: The same dispatch, datelined September 16, adding that Maxwell street station police made the rescue and that this was the first Chicago case in which police were hardly able to save a prisoner from a mob.

framing.detail: Headlines ranged from rescue ('A Negro Murderer Rescued', 'Saved From Lynchers') to the mob ('Negro Murderer Is Almost Torn to Pieces', 'Lynching Bee Barely Averted ... Because Negro Killed White Man'); all called Brinkley a 'negro murderer'.
The Hopkinsville Kentuckian cited the attempt as proof that convicting Danville rioters would not stop mob law and warned of 'a general race war'.
Southern weeklies ran it as a Northern story: the Manning Times headed it 'The Negro in Chicago'.
The Professional World headed it 'Almost Lynch a Negro' and kept the wire's 'negro murderer' and 'done in cold blood' without comment of its own.
